630.bp: Knowledge graphs—vast databases that store facts as connected statements like "Einstein discovered relativity"—are everywhere: powering search engines, question-answering systems, and enterprise data integration. As these graphs grow and change over time, organizations need to understand whether their structure is sound, their schemas consistent, and their contents reliable.
630.wh: Most tools today measure static graphs (snapshots at one moment) or track what changed at the data level only (facts added or removed). What they ignore is the schema—the underlying blueprint that defines what types of things exist and how they relate. A schema drift over time (like categories being added or hierarchies flattening) is invisible to current methods, yet deeply affects how usable the graph is.

MetriKG builds both data-level and schema-level metrics and computes them continuously over time, visualizing how the graph evolves. It measures properties like cohesion (whether related entities cluster together), connectivity (whether entities link to many others), and inheritance depth (how deep type hierarchies go)—all tracked as the graph ages.
630.ww: By tracking both what data changed and how the schema itself shifted, managers can spot when a graph is degrading (fragmentation), when it's becoming overly complex (deep hierarchies growing), or when consistency is breaking. This dual lens—data *and* structure—reveals problems a single view would miss.
630.po: MetriKG offers a web interface to upload RDF files or query SPARQL endpoints, returning a dashboard of metrics over time. This lets teams diagnose data quality issues, track whether merge operations preserved consistency, and set quality thresholds before data corrupts downstream systems.

631.bp: Cloud datacenters run thousands of applications simultaneously, and memory—the fast short-term storage computers use—is often the bottleneck. Disaggregated memory systems share memory pools across many machines using a fast networking protocol called RDMA, letting applications use far more memory than any single box holds.
631.wh: The catch is sharing. When multiple customers' apps use the same disaggregated memory system, they interfere with each other: one app's huge memory request can clog the network, forcing another app's critical query to wait. Existing systems ignore the real topology of datacenter networks and assume applications play nicely—assumptions that break in practice.
631.ap: Wiseswap adds three safeguards. First, it gives memory-swapping operations special priority in the network hardware itself—using RDMA's native signaling—so latency-critical requests cut in front of other traffic. Second, it watches the network constantly and routes memory requests through less-congested paths, like water finding channels around obstacles. Third, it automatically adjusts how much memory each tenant can request based on real-time load, preventing one tenant from starving others.
631.ww: By pushing the fairness and routing decisions into the network hardware (the kernel) rather than relying on applications to be polite, Wiseswap makes interference predictable and controllable. Measuring congestion in real-time and rerouting work ensures that one bad citizen doesn't tank everyone's performance.
631.po: Experiments show Wiseswap delivers 1.3–2.4× higher throughput and 57–73% lower tail latency (the delay that the slowest requests experience) when multiple tenants compete. This means cloud customers get more consistent, predictable performance even when their neighbors are hogging resources.

632.bp: Companies deploy visual models—systems that understand images—onto edge devices like phones, cameras, and robots to run locally without cloud access. But these pre-trained models often fail on new devices because the lighting, angles, or background are different from their training data.
632.wh: Fine-tuning (retraining) a model to adapt to a new environment sounds obvious, but it requires labeled example images from that environment—images with correct answers attached. Collecting and labeling those is slow and expensive. And running the fine-tuning on a tiny device with limited power drains batteries fast.
632.ap: Glasses splits the work: the device sends just one unlabeled image (a photo of the device's real surroundings) to the cloud, which does the heavy computation to figure out how to adjust the model, then sends back lightweight updated weights. The device downloads these tweaks and applies them locally—a much cheaper operation than full fine-tuning.
632.ww: The cloud's computer power solves the two hardest parts—figuring out what adjustments work and doing the math—while the device only handles the quick, final step of applying them. This lets the device adapt rapidly (to a new office, room, or environment) without needing labels or burning its battery on training.
632.po: Testing on two datasets shows Glasses improves accuracy by 5–22% when learning from just one example, and 2–10% with five examples. Models adapt to their deployment environment in minutes, not hours, making it practical to ship a phone camera app that auto-adjusts when moved to a new home or office.

633.bp: The web is increasingly powered by AI—search engines rank results using learned models, streaming services pick songs through recommendation algorithms, and chatbots answer questions. Building systems that deliver these AI experiences to millions of people simultaneously is technically and strategically complex.
633.wh: Scaling AI isn't just about raw compute. It's about balancing latency (answers must come back instantly), freshness (models must track changing tastes), and interpretability (users and developers need to understand why a result ranked first). Most systems sacrifice one for the others.
633.ap: This is a keynote reflection on how AI systems at Spotify evolved: from static search results to interactive, intent-aware experiences where users can steer recommendations, explore new music, and see why suggestions were made. It discusses emerging deployment patterns, tradeoffs, and open problems in system design.
633.ww: Making AI interactive and controllable (rather than black-box) builds user trust and, ironically, improves relevance—users correct misunderstandings in real-time. Intent-aware systems also reduce redundant compute by understanding what the user is really asking for, not just pattern-matching keywords.
633.po: The keynote identifies design challenges for future web systems: how to monitor AI quality in production, how to adapt rapidly to user feedback, how to balance exploration (showing users new content) with exploitation (showing what they'll likely enjoy), and how to do all this at scale. It frames these as open research questions for the community.

634.bp: Simulating human society—modeling how people debate, collaborate, make decisions—is crucial for testing policies, predicting social outcomes, and designing better institutions. The more realistic the simulation, the better we can trust its predictions.
634.wh: Large language models are powerful but naive in multi-agent simulations: they either coordinate too well (everyone agrees, groupthink), deadlock (everyone disagrees, nothing gets done), or follow rigid scripts. Real humans constantly shift between cooperation (pooling knowledge) and healthy skepticism (questioning each other)—a dynamic balance that rigid models can't capture.
634.ap: BEACOF models social interaction as a game of incomplete information: agents don't know each other's skills or reliability, so they form evolving beliefs about peers ("Is this person an expert in medicine? Do they tend to be right?"). Agents then choose how to collaborate (cooperate or critique) based on these beliefs, updating beliefs as they watch peers' performance.
634.ww: By treating collaboration mode as a strategic choice (not a fixed setting), agents become adaptive. A teammate who gives bad advice gets lower credibility over time, so future collaboration tips toward healthy skepticism. A teammate who's consistently right earns trust, so cooperation increases. This mirrors real team dynamics.
634.po: Tested on three scenario types—courtroom debates, open social discussions, medical diagnosis—BEACOF avoids both groupthink and deadlock, converging toward high-quality solutions. Simulations are more realistic and predictions more trustworthy, enabling better policy testing and institutional design.

635.bp: When you read a research paper or legal document on screen, your eye naturally follows structure: scanning the outline, reading sections in order, jumping to a figure when mentioned, cross-referencing tables. Systems that answer questions about such documents should mimic this human strategy.
635.wh: Current document QA systems flatten the document into disconnected text chunks, losing the crucial clues that structure provides: which sections are relevant, how figures relate to nearby text, what the hierarchy means. A figure appearing under "Methods" has different importance than one in "Results," but flat systems treat them the same.
635.ap: DMAP builds a structural map of the document: organizing text into its natural hierarchy (chapters, sections, subsections), linking figures and tables to the text they illustrate, marking cross-references. An agent then reasons over this map: retrieving relevant chunks, checking if enough context was found to answer, and iteratively asking follow-up queries if needed.
635.ww: Structure acts as a filter: it narrows the search space (fewer sections to check means faster retrieval) and as scaffolding for reasoning (knowing that section X is about methodology tells the system which evidence to prioritize). This mirrors how humans read: you don't scan every page, you navigate via structure.
635.po: On benchmark tests of multimodal document QA, DMAP improves retrieval accuracy, makes reasoning more consistent, and reduces hallucination (inventing facts). Practical benefit: a system can now answer nuanced questions about complex documents (research papers, contracts, manuals) more reliably than flat-search baselines.

636.bp: Email marketing at scale—sending millions of personalized messages to the right people at the right time—requires optimizing for multiple goals simultaneously: the business wants engagement, users want relevant content, and resource constraints mean you can't send to everyone or send infinitely.
636.wh: Standard machine learning for recommendations learns what each user likes, but it doesn't handle the constraints (budget, frequency caps, fairness) or the exploration–exploitation tradeoff (show users exactly what they like, or risk missing new preferences?). A pure LP solver can handle constraints but doesn't learn from data.
636.ap: BanditLP combines two pieces: neural Thompson Sampling (a learning algorithm that explores intelligently while learning what works) generates predictions about how each user will respond to each email. A large-scale linear program then solves which emails to send given budget and fairness constraints, at web scale (billions of variables).
636.ww: By decoupling learning (the neural model) from decision-making (the LP solver), BanditLP avoids the brittleness of end-to-end systems. The learning piece improves over time; the solver ensures constraints are always met. The two work together: solver learns which constraints matter most (e.g., fairness vs. revenue).
636.po: Deployed in LinkedIn's email system, BanditLP increases business wins—users open more emails, act on them, and stay engaged longer—while respecting delivery constraints and user preferences. Testing shows consistent gains over simpler methods that either ignore exploration or ignore constraints.

637.bp: AI systems today are reactive: they respond to inputs (questions, images) but don't truly understand the world they're operating in. For AI to collaborate with humans on important decisions—healthcare, education, policy—it needs to reason about cause and effect, goals, emotions, and social norms.
637.wh: Predicting the next word in text or the next pixel in an image doesn't require understanding. But explaining *why* a medical treatment might fail, or why a policy could harm vulnerable groups, requires internal models of physical processes (time, space, causality, action) and human psychology (intentions, beliefs, emotions, values). Current systems lack both.
637.ap: Cognitive World Modeling integrates two models: physical (how the world works—objects move, time flows, actions have effects) and mental (how people think—goals, beliefs, emotional states, social obligations). Together, they form a persistent, evolving representation of reality as humans experience it.
637.ww: An AI with accurate models of physics *and* psychology can reason about consequences—not just predict them. It can say "this action prevents harm to people who care about X" rather than just outputting a recommended action. This reasoning enables explanation, planning, and genuine collaboration.
637.po: Such systems could serve as more trustworthy advisors: they can explain trade-offs, adapt to user values, and predict unintended consequences. Alignment and safety emerge naturally when systems reason about human meaning and context, not as post-hoc patches. This sets a research direction for the next phase of AI development.

638.bp: Predicting the future—whether server load, traffic flow, or website hits—is essential for planning infrastructure and managing resources. Time series forecasting (predicting the next values in a sequence of measurements over time) is a core challenge across the web.
638.wh: Existing methods treat each time step like an independent symbol in text (a token), which works for language but breaks for time series. Time series have structure: today's traffic relates not just to yesterday's, but also to the same hour last week. Treating each time step independently destroys this multi-offset structure, forcing the model to rediscover it from scratch.
638.ap: Time-TK proposes a new embedding method (MOTE) that respects time series structure: instead of encoding each time step independently, it encodes multiple time steps together, capturing patterns that span across different offsets (e.g., hourly vs. weekly cycles). It then feeds these structured embeddings to a novel architecture combining Transformers with Kolmogorov-Arnold networks.
638.ww: By preserving fine-grained temporal dependencies in the embedding, MOTE reduces information loss early in the pipeline. This means the model doesn't have to reverse-engineer weekly patterns from a jumbled stream of isolated tokens; it sees the structure immediately.
638.po: Time-TK outperforms existing methods on web forecasting tasks: predicting traffic spikes, server load, and system throughput. The MOTE embedding is plug-and-play, so it improves any existing forecasting architecture, making it useful for practitioners across different web systems.

639.bp: E-commerce and video platforms constantly introduce new items (products, videos). Recommending these to users is hard because there's no history of who liked them. A new pair of shoes might be perfect for someone, but the system has no way to know because no one has rated it yet.
639.wh: The obvious approach—"find similar users and recommend items they liked"—fails here because it relies on interaction history. With new items, there's nothing to measure similarity against. And not all users are equally helpful: a user who liked three ancient products may not predict current tastes.
639.ap: SuperG first identifies users with truly similar preferences (not just co-viewing history) by examining deep behavioral patterns and multimodal content features. Then it retrieves specifically the informative behaviors: the past actions from similar users that actually predict good future recommendations, filtering out noisy or outdated signals.
639.ww: By disentangling "who is similar to me" from "which of their actions should I learn from," SuperG avoids two traps: spurious neighbors (users who happened to click the same things by coincidence) and uninformative behaviors (old actions that no longer reflect current taste). This two-step filtering surfaces the signal.
639.po: On multi-modal new item recommendation tasks, SuperG outperforms baselines that use simpler similarity metrics or treat all historical behaviors equally. Platforms can now recommend new products or videos more accurately, especially in fast-moving categories where items constantly refresh.

640.bp: Knowledge graphs encode facts over time: "Person X worked at Company Y from 2015–2020." Predicting future facts—"Person X will move to Company Z"—helps systems stay current and fill in missing information.
640.wh: Real knowledge graphs have two layers: individual relationships (local) and long-range patterns (global). A person's job moves show local evolution (one job leads to the next) but also global patterns (tech industry → startup → venture capital is a common path). Most methods capture one or the other, rarely both effectively.
640.ap: DHHGN models both simultaneously: a hybrid hypergraph-graph network captures local patterns (how entities near each other evolve) and high-order dependencies (longer paths that matter). For global history, it selectively boosts attention to pivotal historical facts while still integrating all context, using a gating mechanism to balance local and global signals.
640.ww: High-order dependencies reveal which long-range patterns matter (a 3-hop path in the graph might predict the next fact better than a direct connection). By explicitly modeling these higher-order relationships and adaptively weighting global facts, the system avoids both myopia (ignoring history) and distraction (being confused by irrelevant old facts).
640.po: On standard benchmarks for temporal KG reasoning, DHHGN improves prediction accuracy by capturing subtle patterns that simpler methods miss. Practical benefit: systems can now forecast missing facts more accurately, useful for maintaining up-to-date knowledge bases in enterprise settings.

641.bp: The brain processes information efficiently by sending sparse electrical pulses (spikes), not continuous signals. Spiking neural networks mimic this, using binary signals instead of floating-point numbers, consuming far less power and computation. But spikes sacrifice expressiveness—you lose information compared to real-valued signals.
641.wh: Applying spiking networks to graph data (networks of connected entities) is doubly hard: graphs have irregular structure (nodes have different numbers of neighbors), and spiking signals are binary (on or off). Existing spiking graph networks either add so many real-valued operations that they lose efficiency, or stay so simple that they can't express complex patterns.
641.ap: E2SGNN uses two ideas: dual-scale modulation (global and local real-valued adjustments) applied within the spiking computation, preserving binary efficiency while improving expressiveness. It also adaptively customizes the number of time steps each graph needs based on how complex the data is—simple graphs run fast, complex ones get more time.
641.ww: By modulating within the spike mechanism rather than adding extra layers, E2SGNN keeps the core efficiency gain (addition-only, low latency) while gaining expressiveness. Adaptive latency means no unnecessary computation on easy data, so efficiency scales with problem difficulty.
641.po: E2SGNN efficiently analyzes graph data (social networks, citation graphs, molecular structures) with lower power consumption and latency than traditional graph neural networks, while maintaining competitive accuracy. Useful for edge devices, real-time systems, and large-scale graph processing where computation is expensive.

642.bp: Recommender systems use online experiments (showing different users different things, measuring which ones click) to pick winners. Before deploying a new recommendation algorithm, teams use off-policy evaluation: testing it on historical data without running live experiments, saving time and risk.
642.wh: Off-policy evaluation is tricky. Historical data is biased toward what the old system recommended, so naive evaluation will favor the old system. The inverse propensity score (IPS) method corrects for this bias mathematically, but it's sensitive to randomness: change the random seed or simulation parameters, and conclusions flip.
642.ap: This paper revisits IPS and its variants, testing them not just on synthetic data (controlled experiments) but on real-world logs from the Open Bandit Dataset. It examines how rankings of different methods change with random seeds, sample size, and details of how the historical data was generated.
642.ww: Real data breaks clean mathematical assumptions. Logs aren't i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed)—users who see similar recommendations might behave alike, violating independence. Understanding these violations is crucial because they're what actually causes IPS and its variants to fail in practice.
642.po: The paper shows that seemingly minor choices (random seed, log generator) dramatically shift which estimator looks best, highlighting that off-policy evaluation results are fragile. Practitioners should be cautious about trusting off-policy rankings on a single dataset; validating on multiple data sources and logging strategies is essential.

643.bp: Recommending videos, products, or songs requires fusing multiple types of information: what the item looks like (images, text), what the user's past behavior shows, and what other users liked. Multimodal sequential recommendation (tracking user preferences over time across modalities) is a core problem in modern e-commerce.
643.wh: Simply combining modalities (adding them up or concatenating them) misses synergy: the combination of music genre and album artwork creates a signal stronger than either alone. Also, different users care about different modality combinations: one user picks albums by cover art, another by genre tags.
643.ap: PRISM explicitly decomposes multimodal information into three parts: unique (signals only one modality provides), redundant (signals all modalities agree on), and synergistic (signals that emerge only from combinations). It learns personalized weights for these components based on user history, so each user gets a fusion tuned to their preferences.
643.ww: Synergy isn't noise—it's real signal that naive fusion misses. By explicitly modeling it separately, PRISM can weight it appropriately (some users rely heavily on synergy, others ignore it). This disentanglement also improves interpretability: you can see which modality combinations matter for which users.
643.po: On four recommendation datasets and three different sequence models, PRISM improves accuracy and works as a plug-and-play module. Systems can now recommend more accurately by understanding that certain users are swayed by combinations of features, not just individual signals.

644.bp: On platforms like Amazon or Alibaba, users both search (typing queries) and browse (viewing recommended items). These channels show different intents: a search for "wireless headphones" is explicit, while clicking a recommended shoe is implicit preference. Unifying these signals improves both search and recommendations.
644.wh: The catch is that search intent and browsing intent often diverge (a user searches for work clothes but browsing history shows fashion interests), and improving one task with unified modeling can hurt the other because they compete for model capacity. Static approaches to sharing knowledge break this balance.
644.ap: MinSAR uses VQ-VAE (a method that compresses information into discrete tokens) to fuse long-term user preferences and short-term contextual behavior into a unified interest representation that bridges search (explicit) and browsing (implicit). A separate attention network then dynamically allocates shared knowledge and task-specific expertise based on this unified interest.
644.ww: By generating a unified interest representation from both signals, MinSAR creates a common ground where search and recommendation can be co-optimized without conflict. The attention network ensures each task gets the shared knowledge it needs while preserving task-specific skills—no more zero-sum tradeoffs.
644.po: On two real-world datasets (Kuai marketplace and Amazon Kindle Store), MinSAR improves both search accuracy and recommendation diversity simultaneously, avoiding the typical degradation when joint-optimizing. Platforms can now leverage cross-scenario user signals more effectively, improving experience in both channels.
